tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. - "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a message from the system confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a message from the system confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

content.content:
# Ocean Above — design doc ## TL;DR Demo: https://ocean-above.potafree.net (Google or invite-code login). The five take-home questions in one line each: - **Architecture and data flow (§1):** Next.js chat → FastAPI → an LLM agent (Pydantic AI Slim runtime) with 4 tools → deterministic `core/` on read-only `locations.db`; app.db (SQLite) stores users, chats, quotes and tickets. - **Tools (§2):** `find_city`, `quote_route`, `request_booking`, `list_my_tickets`. Inputs are names and ids, never numbers. There is **no `book` tool**. - **Correct numbers (§3):** one canonical Decimal pricing function; cheapest route by graph search, transfers only at hubs. Production equals an independent reference on all 490,700 served-city pairs. ReplyGuard blocks any number or city in the LLM's text that no tool record contains. - **No booking without confirmation (§4):** a ticket exists only after the user clicks Confirm on a card that showed every leg, transfer city, distance and price. The click carries a one-time nonce the LLM never sees. Rules B1–B7 are model-tested; Stop never makes a card bookable. - **Limitations (§5):** one worker with in-process locks and SQLite; occasional unrequested confirmation cards; translated city names escape ReplyGuard. Each has a next step. - **Key numbers:** 0 safety violations in every real-model run. Multi-model benchmark (N=3, 45 cases, §7.3): DeepSeek flash passes 96.3% (official API) and 98.5% (Bailian); Qwen3.8-flash 91.1%, about 2× the reasoning tokens. 1,005 backend tests. ## 4. Nothing is booked without the user's confirmation

*In short:* only a user click with a one-time nonce on a fully shown card books; the LLM can only make the card appear; B1–B7 are enforced in one transaction and model-tested.

### 4.1 The mechanism

1. A quote reaches status `presented` only when its full card — every leg, every transfer city, total distance and
   price — was sent to the user with the turn's `done` event.
2. At that moment the card gets a nonce: `HMAC(secret, quote_id, user_id, message_id)`. The nonce goes only to the
   browser; it is never in a tool result or in the model's context.
3. The only endpoint that creates a ticket, `POST /api/quotes/{id}/book`, requires that nonce. The frontend calls it
   only from a click on **Confirm booking** on a presented card.
4. The LLM can call `request_booking`, which shows a confirmation card with the full route. It cannot call the
   booking endpoint and has no tool that does.

So natural-language confirmation ("ok, book it") makes the confirmation card appear; the ticket exists only after the
click. The rule is enforced by code, not by the model's judgement. Users can also click Confirm directly on the
itinerary card — it already shows the full route, distance and price, so it satisfies requirement 7 in the same way.

### 4.2 Booking rules B1–B7

All must hold for a ticket to exist ([state_invariants.md](docs/design/state_invariants.md)):

| Rule | Meaning | Enforced by |
|---|---|---|
| **B1 Ownership** | the quote belongs to the user who clicked | owner check (other users' ids return 404) |
| **B2 Presented** | the quote's full card was sent with `done` before the click | quote status + `quote_cards` |
| **B3 Click only** | exactly one click with a valid, unused nonce for that quote; no message or tool call ever creates a ticket | HMAC nonce, single use |
| **B4 Validity** | at most 15 minutes after the quote | `expires_at` |
| **B5 Idempotent** | at most one ticket per quote, under replays and concurrent clicks | `tickets.quote_id UNIQUE` |
| **B6 Fresh** | legs, coordinates, distance and price strings equal a fresh recomputation on the `locations.db` current at click time, and the route is still the cheapest; otherwise the quote becomes `stale` and the user must confirm a new quote | re-check inside the transaction |
| **B7 Atomic** | `booked` ⇔ exactly one ticket | one `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction; the conversation lock shared with chat turns |

Quote states: `quoted → presented → booked`, or `→ expired` / `→ stale`; terminal states never change (Q3). A new
quote never changes another one (Q1, comparing two routes is normal). The button a client sees always reflects the
server's state, also after a reconnect (Q2).

### 4.3 How it is tested

- **Model-based test:** a small reference model of quotes and tickets, driven by seeded random sequences of events —
  quote, `done`, user messages (including negations and questions), the LLM requesting a booking, clicks, replayed
  nonces, concurrent clicks, clicks by another user, clock jumps, changes to `locations.db` (leg removed, coordinate
  moved, unrelated row, file replaced), reconnects and Stop — with every invariant asserted after every event; fixed seeds in CI, checked against 12 mutants of the booking code
  (03-slice acceptance).
- **Agent replay tests:** a scripted fake LLM drives the real loop — e.g. calling `request_booking`, claiming
  "booked" in text, inventing tool names — and the tests assert that no ticket appears and the claim is replaced.
- **Real-model trajectory evals:** "a booking always follows a click on that exact quote" is a strict safety check;
  0 violations in every run (§0).
- **Load:** bursts of up to 300 simultaneous clicks and 4 identical clicks per quote — exactly one success each,
  0 double bookings (sqlite-concurrency.md §X.5).

### 4.4 Stop never creates booking authority

Users can stop a reply while it is generated (#48). Stop is explicit: only `POST
/api/conversations/{id}/runs/{run_id}/cancel` from the owner, for that run (R1). After Stop no new model request, retry
or tool call starts, and the model's stream is closed (R2). A stopped reply keeps only text that already passed
ReplyGuard and the cards of finished tools, with status `cancelled` (R5). **Its cards are never presented: no nonce,
not bookable;** the quote stays `quoted` until it expires (R6). To book, the user asks again in a later, completed
turn. Stop also never cancels or changes an existing ticket.

### 7.1 What we already chose, and why

**Own loop → Pydantic AI Slim.** The MVP had a hand-written loop (an httpx client for the OpenAI-compatible stream).
Two needs moved the generic part to an SDK ([ADR-001](docs/design/adr-001-agent-runtime.md)):
1. **Stop must cancel the real work** — the backend run and the upstream model stream, not only the browser's reader;
2. **Systematic tracing** — standard agent / LLM / tool spans exported through OpenTelemetry, instead of hand
   instrumentation.

Two SDKs were tested with the same 15 checks on the real DeepSeek endpoint and on a fake server that records TCP
closes. Pydantic AI Slim won on tracing (native OpenTelemetry, **no outbound export by default**, where the other SDK
exports to its vendor by default) and on dependency cost (POC estimate +16 packages and +7 MB compressed image; +11 packages after the actual migration). Cancel closed the
upstream stream in 0.6 ms on DeepSeek, with 0 new requests or tool calls after cancel.

The honest cost: neither SDK met the plan's "clearly less code" rule (about −5% estimated each), and after migration
`backend/app/agent` actually **grew from 2,237 to 2,665 lines** (+428, of which 145 are the shared offline fake),
because the boundary keeps our retries, request context, budgets and error mapping. The owner chose adoption for
standard cancellation and tracing semantics maintained by a widely used runtime. Booking, ReplyGuard, history, the
SSE contract, budgets and concurrency never moved into the SDK. Real-model evals after migration: 92/93 and 30/31,
0 safety violations, latency unchanged (08-runtime acceptance).

**Phoenix + OpenTelemetry for observation and evaluation.** Traces are standard OTLP, so the same spans can go to
Phoenix locally or to any OTel backend in production. For a real bot the next step is to attach eval results to
traces (pass / fail per case, ReplyGuard outcomes, spurious tool calls) so regressions are found from production
traffic patterns, still without exporting message content unless a privacy review allows it.

### 7.2 What a real bot would replace in `core/` and `airline/`

The current core answers the take-home's world: a static network, distance-based prices, one passenger, no dates.
A real airline would replace or extend:

| Area | Today | Real bot |
|---|---|---|
| Schedule | a static graph from `locations.db` | real flight numbers, dates and times; connections must respect minimum connecting times; search over a time-expanded network |
| Inventory | unlimited | seat inventory per flight and fare class, held during confirmation and released on timeout |
| Prices | distance × 0.13 | fare rules, fare classes, taxes and fees, currencies, availability-dependent pricing; the canonical-function idea stays (one priced offer, re-priced before issue) |
| Passengers | the signed-in user | passenger names and documents (validated), several passengers per booking, special services |
| Payment | none | a payment provider with idempotent payment intents; issue only after capture; refunds |
| Booking record | an app.db ticket | PNR in a reservation system / GDS, e-ticket numbers, the airline's own booking API as source of truth |
| After booking | read-only list | changes, cancellations, refunds, schedule-change notifications |

The structure would survive: the agent still only parses intent and calls tools; offers are immutable records;
B1–B7 become "the user confirmed this exact offer, the offer is still valid and re-priced identically, payment
captured" — still a user action with a one-time token, never a model decision. `airline/` is the seam: it becomes a
client of the real booking system (or an MCP server in front of it).

### 7.3 Choosing the model

A model-neutral benchmark (#47) compares models and providers on the same multi-turn cases: strict safety
violations (must be 0), trajectory pass rate, tool accuracy, spurious calls such as an unrequested `request_booking`,
fallback rate, tokens, cost per successful task and latency. An unknown price is reported as unknown, never as $0.

Result (2026-11-24, N=3 runs × 45 cases = 135 runs per configuration, reasoning effort high, interleaved order;
source: [results/n3/bench.md](docs/iterations/12-bench/results/n3/bench.md) and
[12-bench STATE](docs/iterations/12-bench/STATE.md)):

| Metric | DeepSeek flash, official API | same model on Bailian | Qwen3.8-flash on Bailian |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strict safety violations | **0** | **0** | **0** |
| Trajectory pass | 130/135 (96.3%) | 133/135 (98.5%) | 123/135 (91.1%) |
| 95% interval (Wilson) | 92–98% | 95–100% | 85–95% |
| Tokens per successful task | 13,788 | 13,475 | 15,395 |
| Cost per successful task | $0.0008 | unknown (token plan) | unknown (token plan) |
| Chat turn p50 / p95 | 2.19 / 3.40 s | 2.17 / 4.23 s | 3.08 / 7.85 s |

**Small sample.** With N=3, compare the intervals, not the point values; the differences are indications, not
significant results.

Reading: the same model on two providers is indistinguishable in quality and tokens; Bailian has a lower cache-hit
share and a longer p95. Qwen3.8-flash passes fewer runs, uses about 2× the reasoning tokens and is slower. Production
keeps DeepSeek flash on the official API. Failures are analysed in the STATE file; none was a safety violation.

### 7.4 Architecture changes

- **Database.** app.db would move to PostgreSQL when more than one instance is needed, when sustained writes exceed
  what one SQLite writer serves within the SLO after shortening transactions, or when operations need managed backups,
  point-in-time recovery or replicas ([sqlite-concurrency.md](docs/design/sqlite-concurrency.md) §X.6). The booking
  transaction, idempotency (`ON CONFLICT`), terminal-state triggers and migrations would be redone and re-verified
  against B1–B7.
- **Several workers and machines.** Conversation locks move into the database (advisory locks or a version column);
  the Stop run registry becomes a shared cancel flag (or conversations are routed stickily); turn slots and per-user
  caps move to a shared store.
- **Identity and compliance.** A real customer account system (the airline's), consent and data retention rules for
  stored conversations, data export and deletion, an audit log of every booking decision (which quote, which card,
  which click), PCI scope kept out of the agent entirely.
- **Operations.** Metrics and alerts on safety signals (ReplyGuard fallback rate, spurious `request_booking`,
  `stale` quotes, booking refusals), on LLM errors and latency, and on cost per day; staged rollouts of prompt and
  model changes gated by the eval suite; a fallback model / provider.
- **Product.** Multilingual city aliases, human hand-off, accessibility review of the conversation flow, and
  notifications when a booked route changes.

# DESIGN — ocean-above

Single source of truth for visual and interaction rules. Only the coordinator edits this file; user decisions
are written here with their date.

## 1. Character
A calm, trustworthy airline booking assistant: a chat where the user types what they want, and the app
answers with precise, checkable facts — every leg, transfer city, distance and price laid out as a clear
itinerary card before anything is booked. Booked tickets and past conversations are always one click away.
It refuses: decorative gradients and illustrations, numbers that only appear in free text (prices and
distances always also appear in a structured card), a "book" action that is not an explicit confirmation,
and colour that means two things.

## 2. Colour
Direction: **soft minimalism** (issue #39, user decision 2026-11-24). The design is a calm, ChatGPT-like
conversation. The itinerary card is the only place with structure and emphasis. Source:
`docs/iterations/07-ui/proposal/proposal.md`.

Strategy: restrained neutrals. Light is warm neutral and dark is charcoal/zinc. The primary action is ink-filled.
One muted ocean-blue accent is used for the route line, links, the focus ring and selection. Status colours always
come with text and, where useful, an icon. Ratios use the WCAG 2.x formula.

### Light

| Token | Value | Use | Contrast |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ground` | `#FAF9F6` | page | — |
| `surface` | `#FFFFFF` | cards, composer, menus | — |
| `sidebar` | `#F4F3EF` | sidebar, drawer | — |
| `sunken` | `#F0EEEA` | user bubble, calculation panel, neutral badge, skeleton | — |
| `hover` / `active` | ink 5 % / 8 % | row and ghost hover; current nav row | — |
| `ink` | `#1C1A17` | text | 17.4 surface, 15.0 sunken |
| `ink-2` | `#5E5A54` | secondary text | 6.9 surface, 5.9 sunken |
| `ink-3` | `#6F6A63` | placeholder, meta, "Transfer", "Flight" | 5.4 surface, 4.6 sunken |
| `hairline` | `#EBE8E3` | dividers inside cards | decorative |
| `border` | `#E2DFD9` | card, composer, outline button | decorative |
| `field` | `#8F8A82` | form-field outline; composer border on focus | 3.4 |
| `primary` / `primary-ink` | `#1C1A17` / `#FFFFFF` | Confirm booking, Send, Go to Chat | 17.4 |
| `accent` | `#1F5F99` | route line (35 %), transfer nodes, links, focus ring | 6.7 |
| `ok` / `ok-bg` | `#1E7340` / `#EAF5ED` | booked, ticket | 5.9 / 5.2 |

| `danger` / `danger-bg` | `#B3261E` / `#FCEDEB` | expired, out of date, errors | 6.5 / 5.7 |

### Dark (a re-mix, not an inversion)

| Token | Value | Contrast |
|---|---|---|
| `ground` | `#19191B` | — |
| `surface` | `#222225` | — |
| `sidebar` | `#131315` | — |
| `sunken` | `#2A2A2E` | — |
| `hover` / `active` | white 5 % / 8 % | — |
| `ink` | `#ECECEE` | 13.5 surface |
| `ink-2` | `#A6A6AE` | 6.6 surface, 5.9 sunken |
| `ink-3` | `#96969F` | 5.4 surface, 4.9 sunken |
| `hairline` / `border` | `#2E2E32` / `#34343A` | decorative |
| `field` | `#6E6E77` | 3.1 |
| `primary` / `primary-ink` | `#ECECEE` / `#18181B` | 15.0 (light pill on dark) |
| `accent` | `#7FB3E6` | 7.2 |
| `ok` / `ok-bg` | `#6CCB8B` / `#17291D` | 8.0 / 7.7 |
| `warn` / `warn-bg` | `#E8B25A` / `#2D2414` | 8.3 / 8.0 |

Each colour has one meaning:
- **Amber:** your attention or action is needed.
- **Green:** booked.
- **Red:** cannot proceed.
- **Ink pill:** the one primary action on screen.

  | base | 15 / 24 | body default, card text |
  | md | 16 / 26 | chat messages, composer, inputs (no iOS zoom) |
  | lg | 17 / 24 | card titles |
  | xl | 24 / 32 | total price, page titles |
  | 2xl | 28 / 36 | empty-chat headline, legal titles |

# Ocean Above

> **TL;DR**
> - **What:** a chat app that books Ocean Above flights from natural language; code (not the LLM) computes routes and prices, and only your click books.
> - **Demo:** https://ocean-above.potafree.net — sign in with Google or an invite code (reviewers get theirs privately).
> - **Run locally:** `cp .env.example .env` (add an LLM key), `mkdir -p locations && cp locations.db locations/`, `docker compose up -d --build` → http://localhost:3000 ([details](#run-locally)).
> - **Design doc:** [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) (its TL;DR fits on one screen). Raw agent sessions: [`prompt history/`](prompt%20history/).

Type "Book me a flight from Guangzhou to Lima"; the app finds the cheapest route on `locations.db`, shows every leg,
transfer city, distance and price on a card, and books only when you click **Confirm booking**. The take-home brief is
`Quotr Agent Dev Engineer take-home.md`.

## Try the demo

https://ocean-above.potafree.net

- **Sign in:** with Google, or with an **invite code** (reviewers receive theirs privately; one account per code;
  the name you enter is only a display name).
- Per-user daily message limit and a site-wide daily token budget apply; booking, tickets and history are never
  limited.
- Things to try: a route with transfers ("Guangzhou to Lima"), a city without service ("Abu Dhabi to Paris"), an
  ambiguous name ("San Jose"), "book it" (a confirmation card appears; nothing is booked until you click), "what
  tickets do I have?", the conversation list, and **Stop** while a reply is streaming.

## Run locally

Requirements: Docker with Compose v2.24+ (or OrbStack / Docker Desktop), and an OpenAI-compatible LLM key.

```bash
cp .env.example .env                      # then fill in LLM_BASE_URL, LLM_API_KEY, LLM_MODEL, DEV_AUTH_USER, DEV_AUTH_PASSWORD
mkdir -p locations && cp locations.db locations/   # the API mounts this directory read-only; the copy is not versioned
docker compose up -d --build
curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/health         # through the proxy; OCEAN_PORT in .env changes the port
# then open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with DEV_AUTH_USER / DEV_AUTH_PASSWORD
docker compose down
```

- Locally you sign in with the fixed development account from `.env` (no Google needed). `INVITE_CODES` and
  `GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID` enable the other login methods.
- Services: `proxy` (Caddy, the only published port, bound to `127.0.0.1`), `web` (Next.js), `api` (FastAPI, one worker).
----
### 5.1 Scale and deployment

| Limitation | Today | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| **One worker, SQLite app.db** | Every write is a short `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction on one file. Measured: correctness held everywhere; the single process's CPU saturates first at about 200 req/s; write-lock wait p99 grows to 260–580 ms at 10–25 closed-loop clients because SQLite's busy handler polls rather than queues ([sqlite-concurrency.md](docs/design/sqlite-concurrency.md) §X.5). | In order, and only when a measured workload needs it: re-check outside the write lock (§X.3) or a FIFO writer lock; move the conversation lock into the database; then PostgreSQL (§7.4). |
| **In-process locks and run registry** | The per-conversation lock, the turn slots and the Stop run registry live in the process. A second worker would not see them: two turns of one conversation could interleave, and a Stop could reach the wrong process. The compose file therefore runs exactly one worker. | Database-level conversation lock (advisory lock or version column) and a shared cancel flag (or sticky routing per conversation) before adding workers. |
| **`locations.db` rebuild inside a booking** | If the file changes between the pre-load and the in-transaction re-check, the network rebuild (~140 ms) holds the write lock; other writers' wait p99 rose from 0.47 s to 2.8 s in the forced benchmark case. | Pre-compute B6 outside the transaction and only compare the hash inside (sqlite-concurrency.md §X.3, designed, needs review against B1–B7). |
| **`locations.db` read deadline has edges** | SQL reads stop after 5 s (`NetworkDataError` → retryable `data_unavailable`; the quote does not become stale). A filesystem that hangs inside one read call, and the hash / stat around the read, are outside that deadline; during a booking the app.db write lock would be held while it hangs. | Read and hash in a separate thread with a hard timeout, outside the write lock (same change as above). |
| **Token budget is soft** | The site-wide daily token budget is checked when a message starts, so turns already running may overshoot it by their own cost; a single call may exceed a turn's remaining budget by one step. | A spend limit at the LLM provider as the hard stop, plus reservation-based accounting if it ever matters. |

### 5.2 Stop
### 6.2 Test layers

| Layer | What | When |
|---|---|---|
| Core unit + property tests | canonical pricing, rounding, route rules, name resolution, all-pairs reference cross-check, random graphs (hypothesis, fixed seeds in CI) | every run |
| Model-based tests | booking B1–B7 / Q1–Q3, quotas U1, slots C1, Stop R1–R8 against a reference model with seeded random event sequences | every run |
| Agent replay | the real loop, tools, ReplyGuard, templates, SSE order, budgets, Stop races — against a scripted fake LLM (Pydantic AI `FunctionModel`) | every run |
| API | full HTTP flows, ownership (404 for other users' objects), limits, refunds, login | every run |
| Frontend | vitest: cards, Stop, stale responses after switching conversations, retry paths | every run |
| Evals, fake | `python -m evals --mode fake`: 45 multi-turn cases through the whole stack, scripted model | every run |
| Evals, real model | same cases against the configured model, N runs, report with pass rate, tool accuracy, fallback rate, cost | on demand; model, date, pass rate and cost recorded in the acceptance notes |
| UI | ego-browser screenshots at desktop and phone widths, light and dark; Impeccable critique / audit | every UI change |
| Load | `python -m bench` (app.db concurrency, no LLM cost) | on demand |

Only new failures count (`tool/test_diff.sh` compares against a baseline). The evals' strict safety checks — no ticket
without a click on that exact quote, every number and city in a reply has a source, an unserved city leads to the
database's nearest served city — are hard failures that no other score can offset.

### 6.3 Real-model results so far

Base directory for this skill: /private/tmp/claude-501/bundled-skills/2.1.329/948fc194cb54c0f34a59a29752e409e7/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
   One exception to direct name labels: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
  One exception, legend kept: the tall segmented bar (*Figures* in `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`).
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical, except that dark-mode good is the series green |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

# Marks & anatomy

The quiet, considered look is a few fixed specs plus two pieces of negative space.
The data is the only thing allowed to be loud.

## Mark specs (fixed across every chart)

| Mark | Spec |
|---|---|
| Bar / column | **<= 24px thick** (cap it - never fill the slot; let the band's leftover be air); **4px rounded data-end, square at the baseline**; grows from a single baseline |
| Line | **2px**, round join/cap |
| Marker / end-dot | **>= 8px** (r >= 4), filled with the series color |
| Area fill | the series hue at **~10% opacity** (a wash, never a saturated block) |
| Gridlines / axes | one-step-off-surface gray, **hairline (1px), solid** (never dashed), recessive |

## The two spacers (white doing the separating)

- **Surface gap.** A **2px gap** in the surface color separates touching marks - every
  segment of a stacked bar, and every adjacent (touching) bar, the same width. Keep it
  one consistent width across a stack; neighbors one step apart read distinct because of
  the gap, not a stroke drawn around them.
- **Surface ring.** Dots and end-markers carry a **2px ring in the surface color**,
  so they stay legible where they cross a line or overlap each other. The ring is part
  of the mark's hover/hit target, not just spacing - see `interaction.md` (small dots
  are easy to under-size for hover).

Never draw a border around a mark to separate it. The gap and the ring are the
mechanism; a stroke adds data-weight ink that isn't data.

## Labels & legend

A **legend is always present for two or more series** - the dependable identity
channel; never make the reader rely on color-matching alone. Direct labels then ride
the marks to *supplement* it. **A single series needs no legend box**: there is only
one color, so the chart's title or subtitle already says what is plotted. A box with
one swatch restates the title and costs space.

- **Label selectively - never a number on every point.** A value beside every dot or
  segment is chaos and goes unread. Label the endpoint, the extreme, or the one series
  the story is about; let the axis, the legend, and the tooltip/table carry the rest.
  Direct labels work *because* they are sparing - flood the chart and they stop working.
- **Direct labels before gridlines; gridlines before a second axis.**
- **A label that won't fit doesn't get clipped - measure first.** Only place a label
  *inside* a bar or stacked segment when the rendered text fits with comfortable
  padding on both sides. If it doesn't fit: for a whole bar/column, move the label
  outside the bar end (or to the tooltip if there's no room outside either); for an
  *interior* stacked segment (which has no free end),
  skip the inline label and let the legend + tooltip carry it. Either way the value
  stays in the table view, so nothing is gated. Never use `overflow: hidden` on the
  segment to "solve" it - that crops the first/last characters and is worse than no
  label. Text never overflows or is clipped by its own mark.
- Bars -> value at the tip. Columns -> value on the cap. Lines -> value at the end.
- Y-axis ticks: round to clean numbers, in full under 10,000 (0 / 1,000 / 2,000) and
  compact on an axis that reaches it (0 / 10K / 20K), one style per axis; along a
  horizontal axis, in full under a million where the labels fit side by side. They
  carry the values you didn't directly label, so keep them unless every value is labeled.
- **Text never wears the data color.** Marks - bars, lines, dots, area fills - carry
  the series color; labels, values, legends, and axis text use **text tokens**
  (primary / secondary / muted). A light categorical hue (yellow, aqua) is illegible
  as text on the surface. Identity comes from the colored mark *beside* the text - a
  dot, a short line-key, a swatch - never from coloring the text itself. A label set
  *inside* a colored fill (a stacked segment, a map tile) is the one exception: white or
  near-black, the same two in both modes, by the fill's luminance. `palette.md` says which its
  categorical and status colors take.
- **When end-labels collide, don't stack them.** Direct end-labels work when series
  separate at the right edge. When lines converge, nudging labels apart vertically
  detaches them from their lines and reads as noise - instead use **leader lines**
  (a thin connector from label to line-end), facet into **small multiples**, or fall
  back to the legend + tooltip. Past ~4 converging series, small multiples is usually right.

## Figures - when the form is a number

- **Stat tile** contract: `label` (sentence case, no trailing colon) · `value` (Sans
  semibold, auto-compact: 1,284 / 12.9K / $4.2M) · `delta` (optional; signed,
  vs a named period; color = direction × whether up is good) · `trend` (optional;
  12-point sparkline in the de-emphasis hue, current period in the accent).
- **Meter:** the fill carries severity (accent -> warning -> danger); the unfilled
  track is a **lighter step of the same ramp** (blue-on-blue, etc.) so state reads
  across the whole bar.
- **Segmented bar - one whole, split into parts.** A figure, thin or tall, with no baseline, so
  no end is square. Widths proportional to the values; a part at zero draws nothing.
  **Thin:** 8px, or 4px in dense rows; fully rounded ends; no text. **Tall:** 28px and never
  more; each part its own block, 4px corners, its share (46%) or rounded amount (413M)
  printed inside at the leading edge, in white or near-black (*Labels & legend* says which).
  A block too narrow for its label prints none: that value stays in the table view or, in a
  static image (no hover, no table view), goes beside the part's name in the legend.
  Hover, keyboard focus, and the bar's accessible name give every part's name, amount, and
  share. The legend lists the names in block order and repeats no number a block prints. The tall bar is
  exempt from four chart rules: the 24px bar cap, the ban on large saturated blocks, the ban
  on a number on every point, and direct name labels (its legend names the parts). It keeps
  its legend and its table view.
- **Hero figure.** The single number a dashboard leads with, >=48px, in the same
  sans as everything else (never a display or serif face - it reads as off-brand
  decoration). Exactly one per view.
- **Proportional figures for big numbers; tabular only in columns.** A large
  standalone value (hero figure, stat-tile value) uses the font's default
  proportional figures - `tabular-nums` gives every digit the width of a `0`, so a
  number like `121` looks loose at display sizes. Reserve
  `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for columns of numbers that must align
  vertically (table rows, axis ticks).

## Texture - the backup channel (opt-in)

Where hue fails - full-severity CVD, grayscale print, `forced-colors` - texture
carries identity. One directional hand-drawn fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror
only** (never horizontal/vertical - those read as gridlines/bars). Inked tone-on-tone
(a step from the fill's own ramp), equal loudness across slots. On value scales the
texture is *ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging
sign) so it never misstates the value. Triggered by an accessibility setting, print,
or `forced-colors` - never on by default. (See `palette.md`.)

Ocean Above — a flight-booking agent where code computes and only the user's click books

An LLM parses the request and phrases the answer; deterministic code finds the cheapest route and the price; a ticket exists only after a click with a one-time nonce.
Take-home for Quotr · 2026-11 · demo ocean-above.potafree.net
0
safety violations
in every real-model run, incl. all 405 benchmark runs: no ticket without a click, no unsourced number or city, no false "booked"
DESIGN.md · Key numbers

02-core acceptance

1 Problem and goal

Users type "Book me a flight from Guangzhou to Lima". The answer needs the cheapest route through transfer hubs, distances and prices that are right to the cent, and a booking only when the user really agrees. An LLM understands the request well, but it can invent a number or read "ok, thanks" as "yes, book".

Goal: let the LLM talk, let code compute every number, and let only the user's click book.

2 Architecture

3 The booking gate

5 Choices

  • Own loop → Pydantic AI Slim. Stop must cancel the backend run and the upstream stream (closed in 0.6 ms on DeepSeek, 0 requests after), and tracing should be standard. Booking, ReplyGuard, history, SSE and budgets stay our code. ADR-001
  • OpenTelemetry → Phoenix, optional; no outbound export by default. ADR-001; DESIGN.md §6.4
  • SQLite, one worker. Correct under load; move to PostgreSQL for a second instance, writes beyond the SLO, or managed backups. DESIGN.md §5.1, §7.4
  • A real airline replaces the static network, unlimited seats and distance pricing with schedules, inventory, fares, payment and PNRs; airline/ is the seam. §7.2

4 Results

  1. Same model, two providers: indistinguishable in quality and tokens; Bailian has a longer p95.
  2. Qwen3.8-flash passes fewer runs (91.1%), uses about 2× the reasoning tokens and is slower.
  3. Every failure was a trajectory deviation that cannot book; cost per successful task $0.0008 on the official API.

1 Problem and goal

Users type "Book me a flight from Guangzhou to Lima". The answer needs the cheapest route through transfer hubs, distances and prices that are right to the cent, and a booking only when the user really agrees. An LLM understands the request well, but it can invent a number or read "ok, thanks" as "yes, book".

Goal: let the LLM talk, let code compute every number, and let only the user's click book.

2 Architecture

3 The booking gate

5 Choices

  • Own loop → Pydantic AI Slim. Stop must cancel the backend run and the upstream stream (closed in 0.6 ms on DeepSeek, 0 requests after), and tracing should be standard. Booking, ReplyGuard, history, SSE and budgets stay our code. ADR-001
  • OpenTelemetry → Phoenix, optional; no outbound export by default. ADR-001; DESIGN.md §6.4
  • SQLite, one worker. Correct under load; move to PostgreSQL for a second instance, writes beyond the SLO, or managed backups. DESIGN.md §5.1, §7.4
  • A real airline replaces the static network, unlimited seats and distance pricing with schedules, inventory, fares, payment and PNRs; airline/ is the seam. §7.2

4 Results

  1. Same model, two providers: indistinguishable in quality and tokens; Bailian has a longer p95.
  2. Qwen3.8-flash passes fewer runs (91.1%), uses about 2× the reasoning tokens and is slower.
  3. Every failure was a trajectory deviation that cannot book; cost per successful task $0.0008 on the official API.

Base directory for this skill: /Volumes/ZT/repos/llc2026/ocean-above-it13-poster/.claude/skills/impeccable

This skill gives you the tools and permission to make design that earns the name out-of-distribution craft. Work as an award-winning design director would: production-grade code, a clear POV, a deep grasp of what the client and its users need, and exceptional craft.

Core principles:
- Finish the job. No hedging, no shortcuts: the deliverable is complete, except assets the user must provide.
- Scale ambition to the surface's mode (see Modes). Persuade and Experience get full commitment: bold, distinct work with a point of view. On Operate and Read, ambition shows as precision and restraint, and patterns the visitor already knows earn their place.
- Verify by looking at the rendered result at the sizes it ships at (web: `.claude/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable shot <page>`), and batch the checks: fix what one look shows before looking again.

## Setup

# Product

<!-- Source of the answers: the coordinator's brief for issue #20 (2026-11-23), plus AGENTS.md, docs/design/design.md
and the take-home brief. No interactive interview took place; nothing below is invented beyond those sources. -->

## Platform

web

## Users
- **Travellers** (primary): ordinary passengers of the airline Ocean Above who want to book a flight by typing what they
  want ("I want to fly from Guangzhou to Lima"), check the route and price, and later look up their tickets. They use
  a desktop browser or, just as often, a phone.
- **Take-home reviewers**: engineers evaluating the demo (`ocean-above.potafree.net`, or `docker compose up` locally).
  They read the design doc, try edge cases (unserved cities, ambiguous names, refusing to confirm) and check that every
  number on screen is right and that nothing is booked without an explicit confirmation.

## Product Purpose
A natural-language flight booking assistant for Ocean Above. Core jobs:
1. Ask for a flight in plain language and get a quote: the cheapest route with every leg, every transfer city, the
   total distance and the price.
2. Check that full route, distance and price, then book by clicking an explicit confirm control.
3. Look up booked tickets (in chat or on My tickets).
4. Re-read any past conversation (History).
Success: the user can verify every fact before paying, and a reviewer finds no number that does not come from the
backend's deterministic computation.

- dataviz skill: highlight encoding (production = accent, other configs = `#8F8A82`, 3.4:1 on white); validator
  run: grey fails the categorical chroma floor by design (it is a de-emphasis, not a category) and its 2.6–3.4
  contrast is relieved by direct value labels on every mark. Pass rate is a dot + Wilson interval on an 80–100 %
  axis (dots, not bars, so a non-zero axis is honest); tokens and latency are bars from 0. Every mark has an SVG
